results.title: How to Install Redis on Ubuntu and Secure It
results.author: Stefan Müller
results.text:
How to Install Redis on Ubuntu and Secure It

# How to Install Redis on Ubuntu and Secure It

 Install Redis on Ubuntu 24.04 or 26.04, choose between the distribution package and the official Redis repository, authenticate with ACLs rather than a shared password, set a memory limit and eviction policy, and verify persistence by restarting. 

Stefan Müller

Developer Infrastructure Writer

- Published September 14, 2026 

• Updated September 14, 2026• 15 min read

#### On this page 

A default Redis install is safer than its reputation suggests — it binds to localhost and refuses outside connections before you touch anything. The risk arrives later, in the changes you make to let an application connect. This guide covers how to install Redis on Ubuntu 24.04 and 26.04, which package source to choose and why that decision matters more here than for most databases, authentication with ACLs rather than a shared password, a memory limit that prevents the OOM killer, persistence you have actually tested by restarting, and the seven failures that put people in a search engine at two in the morning.

## Which Redis you get, and why it matters more here than usual

Start with the version question, because on Redis the answer is unusual: the package in Ubuntu’s repositories is not the default you should reach for.

Redis by source, with upstream support status and licence, checked 2026-09-14

| Source | Version | Upstream status | Ubuntu repo | Licence |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Ubuntu 24.04 LTS | 7.0.15 | 7.0 security support ended 29 Jul 2024 | universe | BSD-3-Clause |
| Ubuntu 26.04 LTS | 8.0.5 | 8.0 security support ends 1 Dec 2026 | universe | RSALv2 / SSPLv1 / AGPLv3 |
| `packages.redis.io` | 8.10.1 | current, actively supported | — | RSALv2 / SSPLv1 / AGPLv3 |

Two independent things are going on, and they compound.

Upstream has moved on. Redis 7.0 reached the end of its security-support window in July 2024, and `7.0.15` is literally the last patch that series received. Ubuntu 26.04’s 8.0.5 is in better shape but its upstream window closes in December 2026 — inside the first year of that LTS.

These packages live in `universe`. Canonical’s standard five-year security maintenance for an LTS covers the `main` repository. Packages in `universe` are community-maintained, and security coverage for them comes only with an Ubuntu Pro subscription (ESM Apps). Check what your own machine is doing with `pro status` before assuming either way.

So for a Redis that holds sessions, queues or cached credentials, use the official Redis repository on either release. This is the opposite of the advice that fits PostgreSQL, where both LTS releases ship a fully supported major — the conclusion differs because the evidence does.

The licence column reflects a separate change. Redis was BSD-3-Clause through 7.2, moved to RSALv2/SSPLv1 in March 2024, and has been tri-licensed under RSALv2, SSPLv1 or AGPLv3 since 8.0 — the last of which is OSI-approved. Ubuntu 24.04’s 7.0.15 predates the change entirely, which is worth knowing if your organisation reviews licences before deployment.

Where Valkey fits. Valkey is the BSD-licensed fork created by contributors after the 2024 licence change, now hosted by the Linux Foundation, and Ubuntu packages it alongside Redis. If you came here to run Redis, run Redis — the two remain close enough that this guide’s authentication, memory and persistence sections apply to either. If the licence is your deciding factor, that fork is worth evaluating on its own terms rather than as a footnote here.

## Install Redis on Ubuntu

Update the system and, if you have not already, allow SSH through the firewall before enabling it:

```
sudo apt update && sudo apt upgrade -y
sudo ufw allow OpenSSH
sudo ufw enable
```

### From the official Redis repository

These are the commands Redis publishes, and they are identical on 24.04 and 26.04 — `lsb_release -cs` resolves to `noble` or `resolute` for you:

```
sudo apt insta

results.title: redis 8.10.2 release notes — security patches & CVE fixes
results.text:
redis 8.10.2 release notes — security patches & CVE fixes

# redis 

 This release includes 2 security fixes for security teams reviewing exposed deployments. 

 Published 26d Caching 

 ✓ No known CVEs patched 

 This release patches 2 known CVEs 

Topics

 +11 more 

 key-value key-value-store messaging no-sql nosql real-time realtime redis time-series vector-databases vector-db 

Affected surfaces

 auth rbac 

## Summary

Security fixes address transaction ACL bypass, unauthenticated cluster bus access, and crashes in TimeSeries, RedisSearch, and Vector Sets.

 Full changelog 

Update urgency: `SECURITY`: There are security fixes in the release.

### Security fixes

- #15673 Commands queued in a transaction could still access keys whose ACL permissions were revoked before the transaction was executed
- #15722 The cluster bus protocol has no authentication of its own unless `tls-cluster` is enabled, so any host able to reach a node's bus port could join the cluster and threaten it. A cluster node now warns at startup when its bus port is left unauthenticated, and the new `cluster-bus-port-protected-mode` option (default `no`) makes refusing to run in that state an explicit choice: set it to `yes` and the node starts only when `tls-cluster` authenticates the bus
- TimeSeries: Prevented Redis from crashing when adding samples to a compressed Time Series key restored from a malformed RDB payload
- RedisSearch: KNN queries on indexes with very long vector field names could cause the server to crash
- Vector Sets: Deeply nested JSON used in Vector Set queries could cause the server to crash

## Security Fixes

- 🔒 #15673 – Fixed transaction commands accessing keys after ACL revocation 
- 🔒 #15722 – Added warning and `cluster-bus-port-protected-mode` option to prevent unauthenticated cluster bus access; requires `tls-cluster` when mode is enabled 

Feedback: hello@releaseport.com

results.title: Redis: persistence, replication, Sentinel and Cluster | Aleksandr Suprun
results.author: Aleksandr Suprun
results.text:
# Redis: persistence, replication, Sentinel and Cluster

2026-09-24

Facts checked against Redis Open Source documentation. The current version as of September 2026 is 8.10 (July 2026). Where behavior appeared in a specific version, the version is noted. Defaults are taken from `redis.conf` of the 8.10 branch.

## Architecture: memory and a single thread

Redis keeps the whole dataset in RAM. Disk is used only for persistence (saving to disk) and does not take part in reads. Hence the main limit: data cannot be larger than memory. The docs say explicitly that a disk backend is not planned.

Commands are executed by one thread. One process serves all clients through multiplexing — one event loop polls all sockets. At any moment exactly one command runs. Commands go strictly one after another.

Plus: every command is atomic, there are no locks. Minus: a slow command blocks all other clients.

What blocks the server:

- `KEYS` — O(N) over all keys. Docs: debugging only, never in application code. Replacement — `SCAN`.
- `DEL` of a big key. Deleting a hash or set with millions of elements frees memory synchronously. The server can stall for seconds.
- O(N) commands on big collections:`SORT`, `LREM`, `SUNION`, intersection of big sets.
- Lua scripts and functions. A script runs atomically. While it runs, other commands wait. After `busy-reply-threshold` (default 5000 ms) Redis answers other clients with a `BUSY` error. `SCRIPT KILL` can stop it, but only if the script has not written anything yet. Otherwise only `SHUTDOWN NOSAVE` is left.
- Mass TTL expiry. If more than 25% of keys with a TTL expire in the same second, the active expire cycle can block the server.

`SCAN` walks keys in chunks through a cursor. Each call is O(1). Guarantee: a key present in the database for the whole iteration will be returned. Downsides: a key may come back several times, keys added or removed during the iteration may or may not be returned. `COUNT` is a hint, not an exact chunk size.

`UNLINK` (since 4.0) removes a key from the keyspace in O(1). Another thread frees the memory. `FLUSHALL ASYNC` and `FLUSHDB ASYNC` do the same. Server-side deletions (eviction, expire, key overwrite, replica flush on full sync) are synchronous by default. They are switched with `lazyfree-lazy-eviction`, `lazyfree-lazy-expire`, `lazyfree-lazy-server-del`, `replica-lazy-flush`. `lazyfree-lazy-user-del yes` makes `DEL` behave like `UNLINK`. All these parameters default to `no`.

source: redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/management/optimization/latency · source: redis.io/docs/latest/commands/scan · source: redis.io/docs/latest/commands/unlink

### I/O threads

`io-threads` are threads for socket work. They read requests, parse the protocol and write replies to clients. Commands are still executed by the main thread.

- Disabled by default (`io-threads 1` — main thread only).
- Recommendation from `redis.conf`: enable on machines with 4+ cores, leaving one core spare. For example, 3 threads on 4 cores, 7 on 8.
- Enable only when CPU is actually short. Otherwise there is no point.
- Redis 8.0 brought a new I/O threading implementation. Since 8.0 I/O threads work together with TLS.
- They do not help against a slow command: `KEYS *` blocks the server with any number of threads.

source: redis.io/docs/latest/operate/oss_and_stack/stack-with-enterprise/release-notes/redisce/redisos-8.0-release-notes · source: github.com/redis/redis/blob/8.10/redis.conf

## Data types and typical tasks

| Task | Type and commands | Caveats |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Cache | String + TTL, eviction by maxmemory | Losing a cache is not losing data. Can run without persistence |
| Counter, rate limit | INCR + EXPIRE in MULTI/EXEC, or a Lua script | INCR without EXPIRE in the same transaction — the key may stay forever |
| Sessions | String or Hash + TTL | A session store needs persistence and replication |
| Simple queue | List: LPUSH + BRPOP | A message is lost if the consumer crashes afte

# USN-8866-1: Redis vulnerabilities

Publication date

6 October 2026

Overview

Several security issues were fixed in Redis.

Releases

 26.04 LTS 24.04 LTS 22.04 LTS 

## Packages

- redis - Persistent key-value database with network interface 

## Details

It was discovered that Redis did not properly manage memory when handling the TLS pending-data list. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to execute arbitrary code. (CVE-2026-81934)

It was discovered that Redis incorrectly handled certain inputs when processing cluster bus packets. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to expose sensitive information or cause a denial of service. This issue only affected Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-92925)

It was discovered that Redis did not properly manage memory when handling the TLS pending-data list. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to execute arbitrary code. (CVE-2026-81934)

It was discovered that Redis incorrectly handled certain inputs when processing cluster bus packets. A remote attacker could possibly use this issue to expose sensitive information or cause a denial of service. This issue only affected Ubuntu 24.04 LTS and Ubuntu 26.04 LTS. (CVE-2026-92925)

## Update instructions

In general, a standard system update will make all the necessary changes.

The problem can be corrected by updating your system to the following package versions:
```

###### high Nessus Plugin ID 350289

#### Synopsis

A database server running on the remote host is affected by multiple vulnerabilities. 

#### Description

The version of Redis installed on the remote host is 8.2.x prior to 8.2.9, 8.4.x prior to 8.4.6, 8.6.x prior to 8.6.6, 8.8.x prior to 8.8.2, or 8.10.x prior to 8.10.1. A remote, unauthenticated attacker may be able to execute arbitrary commands with the privileges of the Redis server. (CVE-2026-81934) - A miscalculated buffer size in CMSketch RDB loading may lead to a heap out-of-bounds write. (CVE-2026-62356) Note that Nessus has not tested for these issues but has instead relied only on the application's self-reported version number. 

#### Solution

Upgrade to Redis version 8.2.9 / 8.4.6 / 8.6.6 / 8.8.2 / 8.10.1 or later.

Redis Vulnerabilities by Version: 6.2, 7.x and 8.x | OSSeva

# Redis Vulnerabilities by Version: CVEs for Redis 6.2, 7.0, 7.2, 7.4 and 8.x

Randall McClure· October 5, 2026· 9 min read

## The short answer

Redis ships each security fix on several release lines at once. In 2026 the fixes have gone to 6.2, 7.2, 7.4 and the 8.x lines from 8.2 upward. According to the version management page on redis.io, 6.2 is supported until 1 April 2027, 7.2 and 7.4 until 1 December 2029, and 8.2 until 1 September 2030. Redis 7.0 reached end of life on 29 July 2024, and its last release, 7.0.15, came out in January 2024. Redis 8.0 is listed as supported until 1 December 2026, yet no 8.0 release has shipped since 8.0.6 in February 2026, so the May 2026 fixes have no 8.0 build. The most serious recent flaw is CVE-2025-49844, a Lua use-after-free that NVD scores 9.9. It is fixed in 6.2.20, 7.2.11, 7.4.6, 8.0.4 and 8.2.2, and never on 7.0.

## Licences, briefly

The version you run also sets the licence. Redis 7.2 and every earlier line are BSD-3-Clause, and patch releases on 6.2 and 7.2 keep that licence. Redis 7.4 moved to a dual RSALv2 or SSPLv1 licence, and Redis 8.0 added AGPLv3 as a third option. Valkey, the Linux Foundation project forked from Redis 7.2.4, stays BSD-3-Clause. For most estates this narrows the upgrade targets rather than blocking them, but it means a move from 7.2 to 7.4 needs a licence review as well as a test plan. See Redis 7.2 end of life for the dates on the last BSD line.

## Security releases since October 2024

Redis publishes most fixes as GitHub security advisories and lists the CVEs in the release notes of every line it patches. This table is built from those release notes.

| Release date | Fixed versions | CVEs |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 2 October 2024 | 6.2.16, 7.2.6, 7.4.1 | CVE-2024-31449, CVE-2024-31228; CVE-2024-31227 on 7.x only |
| 6 January 2025 | 6.2.17, 7.2.7, 7.4.2 | CVE-2024-46981; CVE-2024-51741 on 7.x only |
| 23 April 2025 | 6.2.18, 7.2.8, 7.4.3 | CVE-2025-21605 |

# Debian dsa-6538 : redis - security update

#### Synopsis

The remote Debian host is missing one or more security-related updates. 

#### Description

The remote Debian 13 host has packages installed that are affected by multiple vulnerabilities as referenced in the dsa-6538 advisory. - ------------------------------------------------------------------------- Debian Security Advisory DSA-6538-1 [email protected] https://www.debian.org/security/ Aron Xu October 02, 2026 https://www.debian.org/security/faq - ------------------------------------------------------------------------- Package : redis CVE ID : CVE-2026-23479 CVE-2026-23631 CVE-2026-25243 CVE-2026-81934 Debian Bug : 1147421 1147422 1147423 Multiple vulnerabilities were discovered in Redis, a persistent key-value database, which could result in denial of service or the execution of arbitrary code. This update also includes fixes for several related issues that have not been assigned CVE identifiers: ACL key permission checks for SORT, GEORADIUS, GEORADIUSBYMEMBER, XREAD and XREADGROUP could be bypassed; an out-of-bounds read during ACL key extraction for KEYNUM commands invoked with the wrong arity; missing validation of slot information when loading RDB files; a use-after-free in the blocked client list; an out-of-bounds read in HGETEX; and an integer overflow in the HyperLogLog hash function. Additionally, CVE-2026-66373 addresses an incomplete fix for CVE-2026-25243. Because that interim fix was never released on its own in Debian stable, it is therefore not referenced in the CVE ID list above. This update incorporates the comprehensive fix covering both issues. For the stable distribution (trixie), these problems have been fixed in version 5:8.0.2-3+deb13u3. We recommend that you upgrade your redis packages. For the detailed security status of redis please refer to its security tracker page at: https://security-tracker.debian.org/tracker/redis Further information about Debian Security Advisories, how to apply these updates to your system and frequently asked questions can be found at: https://www.debian.org/security/ Mailing list: [email protected] Tenable has extracted the preceding description block directly from the Debian security advisory. Note that Nessus has not tested for these issues but has instead relied only on the application's self-reported version number. 

#### Solution

Upgrade the redis packages.
